meta.title: ACSAR — CLAU, quantum keys from orbit
meta.description: ACSAR is a student association based in Castelldefels developing CLAU, a 6U CubeSat for quantum key distribution shortlisted for ESA's Design Booster 3.
meta.ogDescription: A 6U CubeSat for quantum key distribution (QKD, BB84 protocol) built by students.

hero.kicker: Association for Advanced and Resilient Satellite Communications
hero.lead: CLAU is a 6U CubeSat taking quantum key distribution to space: an optical channel that generates keys nobody can intercept without leaving a trace.
hero.program: ESA Fly Your Satellite! Design Booster 3

about.p1: ACSAR is a student association based at Campus del Baix Llobregat in Castelldefels [university affiliation pending permission]. We design, build and operate advanced, resilient space communication systems.
about.p2: We are around fifty people and an international community: part of the team comes from outside Spain. We work with concurrent engineering, traceable requirements and real technical reviews — the same framework used to run a professional mission.
about.p3post: : we can offer engineering services to companies in the sector and reinvest the income in our missions, hardware and team training.
about.hq: Base · Room D7-010 · Building D7 · Campus del Baix Llobregat · Castelldefels

mission.p1: Every encrypted conversation depends on a shared secret key. If someone intercepts it on the way, the conversation is no longer secret — and nobody finds out.
mission.p2: Quantum key distribution (QKD) solves this with physics rather than mathematics: the key travels encoded in individual particles of light. Measuring a quantum particle disturbs it, so any attempt to eavesdrop introduces detectable errors. Both parties check those errors and, if there are too many, discard the key and generate a new one.
mission.p3: That is why we call them ultra-secure: security does not rest on how hard a mathematical problem is, but on the laws of physics. A future quantum computer does not break it.
mission.patchAlt: CLAU mission patch: a golden key between two classical faces on a starfield
mission.pb1pre: CLAU is a 6-unit CubeSat in low Earth orbit carrying two complementary links. The
mission.pb1mid: sends the light states that generate the key down to a ground station. The
mission.pb1post: handles telemetry, spacecraft control and the public part of the protocol, where both ends compare notes to distil the final key without revealing it.
mission.pb2post: , the reference standard for quantum key distribution. A pass over the satellite lasts only a few minutes: every design decision — pointing, stability, power and data handling — is driven by making the most of that window.
mission.note: The payload design is confidential. On this site the quantum channel is described at high level only.

cards.p: Six 10-cm units: the smallest viable class that fits the optical terminal and the pointing accuracy it needs.
The reference standard for quantum key distribution, formulated in 1984 and proven on real links.
Quantum optical channel for the key and a classical radio link for telemetry and distillation.
Low Earth orbit, with the ground station at Campus del Baix Llobregat. [orbital parameters to be confirmed]

claims.b: First QKD CubeSat led by a university association in Spain
claims.p: Built by students, with the same engineering rigour as an institutional mission.
Below that size there is no room for the optical terminal and the pointing control a quantum link demands.
Europe's quantum communication infrastructure foresees a space segment; CLAU works towards it at CubeSat scale.

roadmap.lead: CLAU has been shortlisted for Design Booster 3 of the European Space Agency's Fly Your Satellite! programme. This is the schedule up to the end of the programme.

items.p: The team attends the Design Booster 3 training week at ESA's technical centre in Noordwijk, the Netherlands, alongside the other shortlisted missions.
ESA announces which missions continue in the programme after the training week.
Validating the operating principle on a controlled optical bench, with repeatable measurements and component characterisation.
Full subsystem definition, mass, power and link budgets, integration plan and verification plan.
The link leaves the lab: open-air propagation between two sites, with real turbulence and background light.
The programme closes with the mission design consolidated and documented.

how.lead: More than twenty students from several European universities work on CLAU, organised by subsystem around a shared mission model.
how.p: Every subsystem has owners, its own documentation and requirements traceable to the mission objectives. Nothing is considered settled until it can be verified.

subs.name: Power
subs.p: Solar generation, storage and power distribution across the orbit.

subs.name: Attitude control
subs.p: Attitude determination and control: pointing the satellite with the accuracy the optical link demands.

subs.name: On-board computer
subs.p: Flight software, mode management, data handling and spacecraft health monitoring.

subs.name: Radio frequency
subs.p: Classical telecommand and telemetry link, and support for the public part of the protocol.

subs.name: Structure
subs.p: Mechanical configuration of the 6U, interfaces, stiffness and thermal control.

subs.name: Ground segment
subs.p: Receiving station, operations, satellite tracking and processing of the downlinked data.

subs.name: Payload
subs.p: The quantum optical channel. Design details are confidential.

how.cometP: We use ESA's concurrent engineering approach: all subsystems iterate at once on a single mission model. A decision on mass, power or pointing propagates to everyone immediately and its impact is visible right away, instead of surfacing three months later.
how.sprintP: Work is organised in short sprints with verifiable goals and reviews open to the whole team. That lets people with very different course loads contribute without blocking anyone else, and keeps the real state of the project visible at all times.

join.lead: A space mission needs far more than aerospace engineering. If you want to take part, write to us and let's talk.

cols.p: We are looking for people in engineering, physics, computer science and related fields, and also for anyone who wants to help with communication, management or institutional relations. No prior space experience needed: what matters is commitment and wanting to learn by doing.
As a junior enterprise we offer engineering services in communications and space systems, and we collaborate on R&D projects. We also take on specific technical challenges as team projects.
Financial and in-kind support makes the hardware, the laboratory testing and the mission's technical travel possible. Sponsor benefits are [to be defined].
